title: Why Does a Mass Poisoning in 1951 Still Have No Final Answer?
parts: August, nineteen fifty-one.
A small town in the south of France.
People buy their daily bread.
In all, more than two hundred people fall ill.
Some see things that are not there.
At least five of them die.
More than seventy years later, there is still no agreed answer.
Was it a fungus?
A fungicide?
A bleaching chemical?
Or a spy story?
One of these four is only a rumor.
Today we sort them, one by one.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
First, how we work.
We use three seals.
Documented means the sources agree, and we could open them.
Disputed means experts disagree, or the proof is thin.
Myth means it is false.
When we give our own opinion, we say: our reading.
Our sources are old newspapers, a medical letter, history books, and later reviews.
Some we read ourselves. Others we only saw described.
Where we could not, we will say so.
This story involves real deaths, so we will keep it calm.
No sensational pictures. Just the evidence.
Pont-Saint-Esprit sits on the river Rhône, in the Gard.
In mid-August, people begin to feel unwell.
First, nausea and stomach pain.
Then chills, and hot flushes.
Then the visions.
The press later named one night the night of the apocalypse.
Investigators soon traced many of the sick to one bakery.
The flour came from a mill outside the town.
Reportedly, about a hundred people were treated in four nearby villages, earlier in August.
They had eaten bread made with flour from that same mill.
Many patients were taken to psychiatric care.
Most counts say more than two hundred people fell ill.
Five died. Some counts say seven.
Even the number of victims is not settled.
So let's build a clue board.
Clue one. A single bakery.
Clue two. Its flour came from one mill.
Clue three, reportedly. People in nearby villages ate that flour earlier in August.
Clue four. Visions, and a wave of nervous symptoms.
One more clue. Tests on the town's tap water came back negative.
Before the suspects, a quick lesson.
To solve a poisoning, investigators need three things.
A substance. A route into the body.
And a match with the symptoms.
If one piece is missing, the case stays weak.
And bread, once eaten, cannot be tested again.
Suspect number one. Ergot.
Ergot is a fungus that grows on rye and other grains.
In damp years, it can fill a field with dark spurs instead of grain.
In the Middle Ages, it caused outbreaks called Saint Anthony's fire.
It brings burning pain, and it can trigger visions.
Its chemical cousins gave us LSD.
Within weeks, three French doctors wrote to the British Medical Journal, naming ergot.
But scientists in Basel rejected the idea.
Why it fits: visions, and a whole town fed from one source.
Why it troubles people: millers argued the dose needed was too improbable.
And the tests of the time did not agree.
In a newspaper report, a professor says the bread held deadly doses of ergot.
In the same report, a military lab says it found none.
It is unclear whether they tested the same bread.
At first, the authorities kept ergot, and set the file aside for a time.
Verdict: disputed.
Ergot is the oldest answer, and still the best known.
Suspect number two. Mercury.
In the fifties, seed grain was often treated with fungicide.
One of these products, sold as Panogen, contained mercury.
The seed was meant to be sown, not milled.
Some experts suggested it had contaminated the flour.
Mercury attacks the nervous system.
It can bring tremors, sleeplessness, and memory loss.
The judicial inquiry later adopted this as the official conclusion, and called it an accident.
Others rejected that conclusion.
In two thousand eight, a historian published a book in French, called The Cursed Bread.
He wrote that the mercury answer suited everyone.
Business. Politics. Courts. Even science.
Our reading: a convenient answer is not always a correct one.
What fits: nerve symptoms, and a contaminated food chain.
What is missing: a decisive test on the flour that everyone accepts.
Verdict: disputed.
Suspect number three. A chemical in the mill.
Millers once whitened flour with nitrogen trichloride.
In French, it was called agène.
Using it was illegal in France.
Some argue that a mill kept using it anyway.
The same historian saw this as a serious lead.
But he also wrote that it is impossible to prove.
Why it fits: the mill is a clue.
Why it is thin: there is no open proof that it happened.
He saw one more serious lead: toxins from other moulds, little known at the time.
Each one is possible. None has been proved.
Verdict: disputed.
Now the fourth story.
In the fifties and sixties, the CIA ran secret experiments with LSD.
It tested drugs on people, often without their knowledge.
It became public in nineteen seventy-five.
Many of its records had been destroyed.
That part is documented.
The rumor goes further.
It says a CIA program tested drugs on this town in nineteen fifty-one.
But the best-known program began two years later.
So the rumor has to rest on another program.
It leans on a CIA memo and a remark attributed to a Swiss drug company.
We could not open the originals, only second-hand descriptions.
A documented program is not proof of a test here.
We found no open record of such a test.
It is a claim, not a finding.
Verdict: disputed. A rumor, with no open proof.
We do not call it myth, because we cannot prove it false.
Our reading: when records are missing, rumors grow easily.
A good spy story spreads fast because it explains everything.
That does not make it true.
Let's score the suspects against the clue board.
Ergot: strong on visions, weak on tests.
Mercury: strong on nerves, no decisive test.
The bleaching chemical: strong on the mill, thin on proof.
The CIA story: strong on drama, nothing open on this town.
No one scores full marks.
Each suspect explains part of the story.
That is how real mysteries look.
So why is there still no answer?
First, the early tests disagreed.
Second, the fight moved into the courts.
It ran for more than a decade.
Third, even the numbers differ from source to source.
Fourth, the bread was eaten long ago.
Our reading: in a lawsuit, an expert report can become a weapon.
Then answers harden into sides.
Here is what we can say for sure.
Documented: an outbreak, one bakery, and real victims.
Disputed: the cause.
No open proof: the spy story.
So here are the open hypotheses.
One: ergot, in a bad batch of grain.
Two: a mercury fungicide in the flour.
Three: a bleaching chemical, or toxins from other moulds.
Four: something we have not named yet.
A good answer must explain the bakery, the mill, the nearby villages, and the visions.
Our reading: when a case has four answers, be careful with anyone who has only one.
Until one answer does all that, Pont-Saint-Esprit stays open.
Our reading: bread is the food we trust most.
We never inspect it.
That is why this story still bothers us.
Who tested what, and when? That is the question to ask.
Another story where food was not what it seemed.
One more question.
Why did Paris eat its own zoo for Christmas?
